title: Meeting Room Geography
hook: Where people sit in a meeting predicts who will talk, who will lead and who will be overlooked, often before anyone says a word.
why:
Most people choose a seat in a meeting without thinking about it. They sit where there is a space, near someone they know, or in the same chair they took last week. Yet decades of research suggest that seating is not neutral. The shape of a table and where each person sits around it influence who speaks, who is listened to, who emerges as a leader and who disappears.

The chapter on proxemics in Part I introduced Robert Sommer's work on how people choose to sit for conversation, cooperation and competition. This chapter takes that idea into the meeting room. It covers the head of the table, why leaders emerge from some seats and not others, who tends to talk to whom, the seats where people are overlooked, what happens when meetings stand up, what screens on the table do, and the particular problems of meetings where some people are in the room and others are on a screen. The aim is not to win the best seat. It is to see how a room shapes a meeting, and to use that knowledge to make meetings fairer, whether you are running them or simply taking part.

teach.p:
In the 1950s, as part of a large project on how juries work, Fred Strodtbeck and Harmon Hook studied mock juries deliberating around a long rectangular table. Who sat where turned out to matter. Jurors seated at the ends of the table were more likely to be chosen as foreman, and they took part more in the discussion. People with higher-status jobs also tended to take the end seats in the first place, so seat and status reinforced each other.

Later jury research found the same pattern. In a 1985 study, Strodtbeck and his colleague Lipinski found that sitting at the head of the table and having served on a jury before were persistent influences on who was chosen as foreman, and that neither was linked to doing the job better. The seat was shaping the choice, not the person's ability.

The reason is partly visual. The person at the head of a long table can see everyone without turning, and everyone can see them. They are the natural place for eyes to rest when a discussion pauses. Partly it is convention: in most cultures that use long tables, the head is where the host or chair is expected to sit, so whoever sits there borrows some of that expectation.

The figure at the near end of this table has the head. The figure at the far end faces them down the length of the table, the other seat with the widest view. The three along the sides can see the ends easily but must turn to see each other. Before anyone speaks, the room has already given two people an advantage.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if seat position made no difference to who was chosen to lead a group. In jury research, the head of the table was a persistent influence on who became foreman, and was not linked to doing the job better.

teach.h: Leaders emerge where they can be seen.
teach.p:
If the head of the table matters because of what it lets people see, then the effect should appear even without a head of the table. In 1962 Lloyd Howells and Selwyn Becker tested this. They seated groups of five at a rectangular table, with two people on one side and three on the other, and gave them a task to discuss. Nobody was appointed as leader.

Leaders were more likely to emerge from the side with two people. The researchers' explanation was visual access. Each person on the two-person side could look across at three people without turning, while each person on the three-person side faced only two. Being able to see and be seen by more of the group seems to make it easier to speak often, to be listened to and to direct the discussion.

The lesson extends beyond rectangular tables. In any group, the person whose position lets them catch the most eyes has an advantage in getting the floor. In a lecture theatre, it is the person at the front. At a dinner, it is often the person in the middle of a long side. In a circle of chairs, nobody has much of an advantage, which is one reason circles are used when people want discussion to be more equal.

This cuts both ways. If you want to contribute, choose a seat from which you can see most of the group. If you are running a meeting and want to hear from everyone, notice who has been seated where they can barely see the others, and bring them in. The figure here sits forward, engaged, in a seat with a clear view of the room.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if leaders were equally likely to emerge from any seat. In Howells and Becker's study, they emerged more often from the side where each person could see more of the group.
teach.pullQuote: Before anyone speaks, the room has already given some people an advantage.

teach.p:
In 1950 the psychologist Bernard Steinzor noticed something about the flow of conversation in discussion groups seated in a circle. People tended to respond to the person sitting opposite them more than to the people beside them. When someone finished speaking, the next speaker was often the person facing them across the group. This became known as the Steinzor effect.

The likely reason is the same as before: you can see the face and body of the person opposite, so their words land more fully and their pauses invite you in. The people beside you are hard to see without turning your head, so their contributions are easier to let pass.

Sommer's work, discussed in Part I, adds another layer. People who expect to compete tend to sit opposite each other, and people who expect to cooperate tend to sit side by side. Sitting directly across from someone can therefore feel like an invitation to debate, while sitting beside them can feel like being on the same side. Neither is fixed. But it is worth knowing that the seat opposite a person is the one most likely to start an exchange, friendly or otherwise.

In practice, this means you can use seating to shape the conversation. If you want to work through a disagreement with a colleague, sitting at a corner, at right angles, often feels less confrontational than sitting directly across. If you want to back someone's proposal, sitting beside them shows it. And if two people keep clashing in a meeting, it may help, quietly, to stop seating them face to face. The figures here sit across a table from each other, the arrangement most likely to set off an exchange.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people in a group were as likely to respond to their neighbours as to the person opposite. Steinzor's observations suggested they responded more to those they could see directly.

teach.p:
If some seats give power, others take it away. In most meeting rooms, three kinds of seat are easy to overlook.

The first is the seat beside the chair. It looks like a position of favour, but the person who sits there is hard for the chair to see without turning. They can be ignored without anyone meaning to ignore them. The second is the far corner of a long side, where the person is out of the natural line of sight of both ends. The third is the row of chairs against the wall, where junior staff, assistants and latecomers often sit. People there are physically outside the meeting, and they are rarely asked to speak.

These seats are often taken by the people who are already least likely to speak: those who are new, junior, quiet or unsure of their place. The room then confirms their silence. Some people choose the edges deliberately because they feel safer there, and that is their right. But it is worth noticing when the same people end up on the edges every week.

There are simple remedies. If you are running a meeting, make enough space at the table for everyone, so nobody sits against the wall. Look around the whole table before moving on, including the seats nearest you. Ask the person in the corner for their view by name. If you are the one who usually takes an edge seat, try a seat with a clear view of the group, and notice whether you speak more. The figure here takes notes, head down, the role that often comes with a seat at the edge.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people seated at the edges of a meeting were asked to contribute as often as those at the centre. In many meetings they are not, which is why a chair needs to look deliberately around the whole room.

teach.p:
Most meetings are held sitting down, but the evidence on standing meetings is intriguing. In 1999 Allen Bluedorn, Daniel Turban and Mary Sue Love had groups of five make a decision either sitting down or standing up. The standing meetings were about a third shorter, and the decisions they reached were no worse. People in the standing groups were, however, less satisfied with the meeting, and the meetings in the study were short, so the results may not apply to long or complicated discussions.

In 2014 Andrew Knight and Markus Baer looked at what standing does to a group. Groups of students spent half an hour making a short recruitment video for their university, either in a room with chairs around a table or in a room with no chairs. The groups without chairs were more physiologically aroused, as measured by sensors on their wrists, and less territorial about their ideas. They shared more information, built on each other's contributions more, and produced better videos.

These are laboratory studies, and standing is not possible or comfortable for everyone, including people with disabilities, pain or fatigue. But they suggest that a table and chairs are not neutral either. Sitting at a table encourages people to claim and defend their own patch, while standing loosens that.

A short standing check-in, a few people round a whiteboard, or a walk instead of a seated one-to-one can change the feel of a discussion. The figures here stand in a loose group of three, close enough to share ideas, with no table to divide them into territories.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if standing groups shared no more information than seated groups. In Knight and Baer's study they shared more and were less territorial about ideas, though the study was a short laboratory task.

teach.p:
Few meeting rooms are free of screens. Laptops are open in front of people, phones lie face up beside coffee cups, and somebody is always checking something. What do they do to a meeting?

The evidence on phones is more uncertain than popular articles suggest. In 2013 Andrew Przybylski and Netta Weinstein reported that the mere presence of a phone on the table made strangers' conversations feel less close and trusting. It is often cited, but two later attempts to repeat the study found no such effect, so the claim that a phone on the table by itself spoils a conversation is, at best, unproven.

The evidence on laptops is clearer, though it comes from classrooms. In 2013 Faria Sana, Tina Weston and Nicholas Cepeda found that students who multitasked on laptops during a lecture remembered less, and so did students sitting where they could see someone else's screen. Distraction spread to the people nearby. A meeting is not a lecture, but the principle probably carries over: an open laptop showing email draws the eyes of the person using it and of those around them.

What is clearest is how screens are read. Someone looking down at a phone while others speak is seen as absent, however much they are listening. In a meeting where your attention matters, close the laptop unless you need it, put the phone away rather than face down on the table, and take notes on paper if you can. The figure here looks down at a phone, in the meeting but not of it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if multitasking on a laptop had no effect on the people sitting nearby. In Sana and colleagues' classroom study, those who could see a multitasker's screen remembered less of the lecture.

teach.p:
Meetings where some people are in a room and others join by video have become common, and they bring a particular imbalance. The people in the room can see each other's faces, hear each other's small sounds and catch each other's eye. The people on the screen see a wide shot of a table, often from one end, and hear a room's worth of voices through a single microphone. They are the overlooked seats of the modern meeting.

The usual pattern is that the room talks to itself. Conversation flows between the people at the table, the screen becomes a background, and remote colleagues struggle to find a gap to speak in. Because of the delay, by the time they unmute, the moment has passed. The chapters on video calls and audio earlier in this part looked at why. Here the question is what the room can do about it.

A few practices help. Some teams have everyone, including those in the room, join from their own laptop, so every face is the same size and every voice has its own microphone. Others put the camera at the end of the table facing the room, and the screen where the people in the room can see it without turning. Many chairs ask remote colleagues to speak first on each item, before the room's conversation takes off, or appoint someone in the room to watch the screen for raised hands.

None of this is complicated, but it has to be done on purpose, because the room's geography works against it. The figure here is on a video call, alone in a frame. In a hybrid meeting, that frame is the far corner of the table, and someone needs to keep looking at it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if remote participants in hybrid meetings spoke and were listened to as easily as those in the room. In most hybrid meetings they are not, which is why chairs need deliberate practices to include them.

poseGallery.annotation: However much you are listening, looking down at a phone reads as being absent. Put it away, not just face down.

poseGallery.doCaption: Leaning in from a seat with a view
poseGallery.annotation: Edge seats confirm silence. A seat from which you can see most of the group makes it easier to speak and be heard.

caseStudy:
Daniel, forty-one, became head of a design department and inherited a weekly meeting of eleven people around a long table. Within a month he noticed that the same three senior designers did almost all the talking. One of them, Graham, always sat at the far end, facing the chair. The three newest members of the team sat in chairs against the wall, and the two colleagues who joined from another office appeared on a screen at one end of the room that Daniel had to turn round to see.

He made a few changes. He asked facilities for more chairs at the table, so nobody sat against the wall. He stopped sitting at the head and took a seat in the middle of one long side, from which he could see almost everyone. He moved the screen so it faced him, and on each item he asked the remote colleagues to speak first. He asked people to put phones in their bags, and laptops stayed closed unless someone was presenting.

Not everything worked. Graham was irritated that the meeting no longer seemed to have a head, and said so. One of the remote designers found being asked first uncomfortable and asked Daniel to stop singling her out, so he switched to a quick round of everyone instead. But within six weeks, Femi, a junior designer who had not spoken in a single meeting, presented an idea that the team adopted.

Daniel does not know how much was the seating and how much was simply that he had started asking. He suspects the two worked together: the room made asking natural, and asking made the room feel open. He also started a fifteen-minute standing check-in on Monday mornings, which people grumbled about at first and now defend.
observe: Notice where people sit in your next meeting, and who speaks most from which seats.
Notice who responds to whom: whether the next speaker is usually the person opposite, beside or at the head.
Notice who sits at the edges of meetings week after week, and whether they are ever asked to speak.
In a hybrid meeting, notice how often the people in the room look at the screen, and how long remote colleagues wait to be heard.

drills.name: Seat Map
steps: In your next meeting of five or more, sketch the table and mark where each person sits.
During the meeting, put a tally mark by each person every time they speak.
Afterwards, compare the tallies with the seats: heads, ends, sides, corners and wall.
Note whether the person who spoke most had the widest view of the group.
Write one change to the seating you would try next time.
variations: Map the same regular meeting for three weeks running, and see whether the people who speak most stay in the same seats.
Add arrows to your seat map showing who responds to whom, and look for the Steinzor pattern of people answering whoever sits opposite.
Map a hybrid meeting, including the people on the screen, and compare their tallies with those of people in the room.

drills.name: Choose Your Seat
steps: Before your next meeting, arrive a few minutes early.
Choose a seat from which you can see most of the people who will attend.
During the meeting, notice how easy it is to catch eyes and to find a gap to speak.
Compare it with how you usually feel in your normal seat.
Decide whether to keep the new seat.
variations: Try sitting opposite the chair in a meeting where you usually sit beside them, and notice whether you are addressed more often.
Sit side by side with a colleague you usually face across the table, for a working session, and notice whether the tone changes.
In a meeting where you usually speak a lot, take a corner seat for once, and notice how hard it is to get the floor from there.

drills.name: Bring in the Edges
steps: If you run a meeting, look around the whole table before closing each item, including the seats nearest you.
Ask one person at the edge, or on the screen, for their view by name.
If someone is sitting against the wall, invite them to the table.
Afterwards, note who spoke who usually does not.
variations: Keep a written list of who has spoken in your next meeting, and before each decision, invite one person who is not on it.
Rearrange a regular meeting into a horseshoe or a circle for one week, and ask people afterwards whether it felt different.
If you are not the chair, invite one quiet colleague into the discussion yourself: "I'd like to hear what Femi thinks about this."

drills.name: Standing Check-in
steps: Choose a short, regular meeting, such as a weekly update, and try holding it standing up.
Keep it to fifteen minutes and a single purpose.
Offer chairs to anyone who prefers or needs to sit.
After two or three weeks, ask people whether it felt different, and how.
Keep it, change it or drop it based on what they say.
variations: Put stools or chairs around the standing table from the start, and use one yourself on some days, so that sitting is clearly normal.
Try a walking meeting for a one-to-one, with a seated option offered beforehand, and compare it with the same conversation at a desk.
Time the standing meeting for three weeks and the sitting version for three weeks, and compare the length and what got decided.

quiz.q: A colleague says the person who ends up chairing a group is usually the most capable, wherever they happen to sit. What does jury research suggest?
options: Seat made no difference, because jurors always chose the most experienced among them
Jurors chose the youngest person as foreman, whatever seat he or she had happened to take
Seat position influenced who became foreman, and it was not linked to doing the job better
Only jurors who sat in the middle of a long side were ever chosen to be the jury foreman
quiz.explain: Jurors at the ends of the table were more likely to be chosen and took part more. Strodtbeck and Lipinski found that head-of-table seating remained an influence and was unrelated to how well the person did the job.

quiz.q: In Howells and Becker's study, five people sat at a table with two on one side and three on the other. Where did leaders tend to emerge?
options: From the side with two people, who could see more of the group
From the side with three people, who had more allies close by
Equally from both sides, because nobody had been appointed leader
From whoever arrived first, regardless of where they ended up seated
quiz.explain: Each person on the two-person side could see three people without turning. Being able to see and be seen by more of the group seems to make it easier to take and hold the floor.

quiz.q: What did Steinzor notice about the flow of conversation in discussion groups seated in a circle?
options: People spoke mainly to those sitting immediately to their right
People responded to whoever had spoken loudest, wherever they sat
People mostly spoke in a fixed order going round the circle
People tended to respond to the person sitting opposite them
quiz.explain: Steinzor found that the next speaker was often the person facing the last one. You can see the face and body of someone opposite, so their words land more fully and their pauses invite a reply.

quiz.q: What did Knight and Baer find when groups worked in a room without chairs?
options: They argued more and produced worse work, because standing made them tired
They were less territorial about ideas and shared more information with each other
They finished faster but shared fewer ideas and produced much weaker videos
They behaved in exactly the same way as groups seated around a table
quiz.explain: Standing groups were more aroused and less territorial about their ideas. They shared more information and produced better videos, though the study was a short laboratory task.

quiz.q: A friend tells you that simply having a phone on the table ruins a conversation. What is the best summary of the evidence?
options: Every study has confirmed it, so phones should always be banned from tables
The original study found this, but later attempts to repeat it did not
Phones on tables improve conversations, because they make people feel safe
The effect has been found only when the phone rings during the conversation
quiz.explain: Przybylski and Weinstein reported the effect in 2013, but two later replications found no effect on conversation quality. Looking at a phone while someone speaks is still read as absence, which is a separate matter.

quiz.q: You are chairing a hybrid meeting with six people in the room and three on a screen. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask remote colleagues to speak first on each item, and keep the screen in your view
Let the room talk freely and ask the remote colleagues to raise any points by email
Seat yourself with your back to the screen, so the room can concentrate on its own discussion
Ask the remote colleagues to keep their cameras off, to save on bandwidth and distraction
quiz.explain: In hybrid meetings the room tends to talk to itself. Inviting remote colleagues in first, and keeping them in view, works against the geography of the room.

quiz.q: What did Strodtbeck and Lipinski's 1985 study suggest about sitting at the head of a jury table?
options: It had no influence at all on which of the jurors the others chose to be their foreman
It influenced who was chosen as foreman, but was not linked to doing the job better
It made jurors less likely to be chosen, because it looked as if they wanted power
It mattered only for jurors who had served before and knew how the process worked
quiz.explain: Sitting at the head of the table was a persistent influence on who was chosen as foreman, but it was not linked to doing the job better. The seat was shaping the choice, not the person's ability.

quiz.q: Two managers who dislike each other always sit directly opposite one another, and every meeting turns into a duel. What fits this chapter best?
options: Accept the duels, since seating cannot change how two people feel about each other
Try seating them side by side for joint work, facing the same problem rather than each other
Seat each of them beside the chair, so that neither of them can easily be seen or heard by the room
Hold the meeting standing up, since standing groups are always less argumentative
quiz.explain: People who expect to compete tend to sit opposite each other, and people respond most to whoever faces them. Side by side, facing a shared task, makes cooperation easier to start, though seating is never the whole story.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a laptop in a meeting only distracts the person using it. What did Sana, Weston and Cepeda find in their classroom study?
options: That laptops helped everyone remember more, because notes were faster to take
That students who could see someone else's screen also remembered less of the lecture
That laptops made no difference to what students remembered from the lecture
That only students who used laptops for games, not email, were distracted by them
quiz.explain: Students who multitasked on laptops remembered less, and so did students sitting where they could see someone else's screen. Distraction spread to the people nearby.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific meeting you attend regularly. Sketch where people usually sit, including anyone on a screen or against the wall. Who speaks most, and from which seats? Where do you usually sit, and how easy is it for you to be seen and heard from there? Describe one change, to your own seat or to the room, that might make the meeting fairer, and what you expect would happen if you tried it.
reflection.guidance: You do not need to be in charge to notice how a room shapes a meeting, and small changes, like choosing a different seat, are within anyone's reach. Be specific about the layout, including the table, the screen and the door. If you run the meeting, think about who is on the edges and why.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat seating as neutral, when the head of a table and seats with a wide view give some people an advantage before anyone speaks. The second is to read the person at the head as the natural leader, when the seat may be doing much of the work. The third is to let the same quiet people end up on the edges and against the wall every week, then conclude that they have nothing to say. The fourth is to run a hybrid meeting as if the people on the screen were in the room, when they are in fact the most overlooked seat of all. The fifth is to turn seating into a game of advantage, competing for the best chair, when the more useful skill is arranging a room so that everyone can be seen and heard.

moreCases.title: The chair who arrived late
moreCases.scene:
Joyce, sixty-seven, a retired head teacher, moves into a block of flats where the residents have just formed an association to deal with a
  long-running dispute about repairs. She goes to the first meeting in the community room on the ground floor, arriving ten minutes late because her
  bus was delayed. Eighteen people are already sitting around three tables pushed together into a long rectangle. The only free chair is at the far
  end, facing the door.

  She sits down, apologises and listens. Because she is at the end of the table, everyone can see her and she can see everyone. When the discussion
  stalls, people's eyes drift towards her, and she finds herself summarising what has been said and suggesting next steps, as she used to in staff
  meetings. At the end of the evening, when someone proposes electing a chair, three people suggest her. She is elected by a show of hands.

  On the way back to her flat, a man called Tunde, who has lived in the block for twelve years and has been fighting the landlord about the repairs
  for most of them, tells her, quite pleasantly, that he had been hoping to chair it himself. He had sat on the long side, by the radiator, and had
  spoken twice.

  Joyce lies awake that night. She knows almost nothing about the dispute. Tunde knows everything.

She also remembers that, as a head teacher, she had always sat at the end of the staff-room table, and that her deputies had sometimes complained that meetings felt like assemblies.

At the meeting, she had noticed that a man by the radiator kept starting to speak and stopping when someone nearer the ends got in first. She had not connected it with the table. She had assumed he was shy.
moreCases.misread:
The residents read Joyce's position at the end of the table, and the summaries it made easy for her to give, as natural leadership. Joyce, at first, read her election as recognition of her ability, and did not consider how much the seat had done.

Tunde, too, read the vote as a judgment on him, and nearly stopped coming.

The residents who voted also read their own choice as a judgment of the candidates, when it was largely a response to the person who had been easiest to see and hear all evening. None of them would have said that the seat decided it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Strodtbeck and Hook found that jurors at the ends of a long table were more likely to be chosen as foreman, and later work found that the seat shaped the choice without being linked to doing the job better. Joyce's chair gave her the widest view in the room and made her the natural resting place for eyes when the discussion paused. Tunde, on the long side by the radiator, was out of most people's line of sight. Joyce's better response was to say so. At the next meeting she explained that she had been elected largely because of where she happened to sit, proposed that Tunde lead on the repairs dispute, which he knew best, and suggested arranging the tables in a horseshoe in future, so that nobody had the end seat. The association voted for both. Joyce stayed on as secretary, which she said suited her far better.

Tunde later told her that the horseshoe had done more for the association than either of them.

moreCases.title: The deputy beside the head
moreCases.scene:
Nikhil, thirty-nine, is deputy head of a large secondary school. Every Monday morning the senior leadership team meets in the head teacher's
  office, around an oval table. The head, Sarah, sits at the end nearest the window, and Nikhil has always sat in the chair immediately to her right,
  where he sat on his first day because it seemed the natural place for a deputy.

  Over the past term he has begun to feel sidelined. Sarah seems to address most of her questions to the two assistant heads sitting opposite her
  and further down the table. When Nikhil speaks, she often carries on looking at them, and once or twice she has asked one of them what they think
  of a point he has just made, as if he had not made it. He has started to wonder whether she is losing confidence in him, or preparing to bring in
  someone else.

  He raises it, carefully, with a former colleague who is now a head elsewhere. She asks him to draw the table and show her where everyone sits. Then
  she asks him how often Sarah would have to turn her head to look at him.

  He thinks about it. Sarah would have to turn almost ninety degrees. The assistant heads are in front of her without her moving at all.

He has also noticed that the assistant heads sometimes glance at each other when he speaks, and has read it as a shared judgment of his ideas. It may simply be that they can see each other and cannot easily see him.

In meetings with outside visitors, Nikhil sits wherever there is space, and he has noticed that Sarah turns to him readily then. He had put it down to her wanting to show a united front.
moreCases.misread:
Nikhil read Sarah's habit of looking past him as a loss of confidence in him, and began to fear for his job. The assistant heads, without thinking about it, read the direction of Sarah's attention as a sign of who mattered most at the table.

Sarah, for her part, had read Nikhil's quietness as contentment, and had no idea that he felt sidelined.

He also read the assistant heads' greater share of the conversation as a sign that Sarah preferred them, rather than as the natural result of being in front of her eyes.
moreCases.betterRead:
The seat beside the chair looks like a position of favour, but it is one of the hardest seats in the room to be seen from. Steinzor found that people tend to respond to whoever sits opposite them, because they can see that person's face and body. Sarah was not turning away from Nikhil; she was looking straight ahead. His former colleague's better suggestion was to change the seat before reading anything into the relationship. The next Monday, Nikhil took the chair at the far end of the oval, opposite Sarah. Within two weeks she was turning to him first on most items, and when he mentioned the change to her over coffee, she laughed and said she had wondered why he had suddenly become so much more vocal.

He also suggested to Sarah that the assistant heads rotate seats too, so that nobody became the person beside the head by default.

moreCases.title: The rivals across the table
moreCases.scene:
Gemma, forty-four, and Lewis, forty-seven, run the two largest sales regions of a building supplies company. They are both very good at their
  jobs and they do not like each other. At the monthly regional meeting, around a long table, they always sit directly opposite each other, in the
  middle of the two long sides, as if by appointment.

  Every meeting becomes a duel. When Gemma speaks, Lewis answers, usually to disagree. When Lewis makes a proposal, Gemma picks it apart. The other
  managers have learned to keep their heads down until the exchange has run its course. The managing director, Andy, has started to dread the
  meetings and to make the important decisions afterwards, privately, with each of them separately.

  This quarter the company needs a joint plan for a new national customer, whose stores fall in both regions. Andy has asked Gemma and Lewis to
  produce it together, and he expects it to fail. Before their first planning session, his assistant, Hana, sets up the small meeting room. She is not
  thinking about psychology. The big table is booked, so she puts two chairs side by side at a narrow desk facing a whiteboard, with a single laptop
  between them.

  Gemma and Lewis arrive, look at the chairs, and sit down next to each other, because there is nowhere else to sit.

The other managers have their own seats too, arranged in a rough pecking order down the table. The newest, a regional manager called Priti, sits by the door, where she has to lean forward to see either of the duellists.

Andy has tried asking them both to "keep it constructive". Each of them has taken it as a rebuke aimed at the other.
moreCases.misread:
Andy and the other managers read the duels as a clash of personalities that nothing could change. Gemma and Lewis each read the other's constant opposition as hostility, and neither noticed how much the seats were inviting it.

Andy had also read his private decision-making as a sensible workaround, when it was teaching both managers that the duel was the real meeting.

Priti, at the far end by the door, read the duels as the way the company did things, and learned to stay quiet. The meeting was teaching every newcomer the same lesson.
moreCases.betterRead:
Sommer found that people who expect to compete tend to sit opposite each other, and people who expect to cooperate tend to sit side by side; Steinzor found that people respond most to whoever faces them. Gemma and Lewis's habitual seats set them up for an exchange every time either spoke. Side by side, facing the same whiteboard and the same laptop, they were looking at the problem rather than at each other. The planning session ran for two hours and produced a plan that both of them liked. Nobody believed it was the chairs alone. But Andy's better reading, once he heard about it, was that the arrangement had made cooperation easier to start, and he began to mix the seating at the monthly meeting, with name cards, rotating every month. The duels did not stop entirely. They became shorter.

Priti, at the next meeting, sat in the middle of a long side for the first time, and spoke three times.

Gemma and Lewis never became friends. But the joint plan won the account, and both of them took the credit, which Andy decided was a fair outcome.

moreCases.title: The stool at the stand-up
moreCases.scene:
Kirsty, thirty-six, is a data analyst at an insurance company. Her new team leader, Ollie, is enthusiastic about standing meetings, which he
  has read make teams faster and more creative. He introduces a fifteen-minute stand-up every morning at nine, around a high table in an open area.
  There are no chairs. He says it keeps things snappy.

  Kirsty has a chronic condition that causes fatigue and pain in her joints, and standing still for fifteen minutes first thing in the morning is
  hard for her. She has not told Ollie, because she has only just joined the team and does not want to be known for her health. For the first week
  she stands and grits her teeth. In the second week she brings a stool from her desk and perches on it at the edge of the group, a little lower than
  everyone else and slightly behind them.

  Ollie notices. To him, the stool looks like a statement that she is not bought into the new routine. A colleague jokes, kindly, about Kirsty
  "taking a seat at the back". In the stand-ups she starts speaking less, because from the stool she is looking up at a ring of backs and elbows.

  In her first one-to-one, Ollie tells her that he wants everyone to feel part of the team, and asks her whether she is finding the stand-ups useful.
  She is not sure what to say.

She has also noticed that the stand-ups have become slightly shorter for everyone else and slightly harder for her, and that nobody seems to see the second part.

Ollie, for his part, is pleased with the stand-ups. They are quicker than the old sit-down meetings, and the team seems more energetic. He has not asked anyone how they find them, because they seem to be going so well.
moreCases.misread:
Ollie read Kirsty's stool, at the edge of the group, as reluctance to buy into his new routine. Kirsty read his question in the one-to-one as a warning that she was being seen as difficult, and nearly said that everything was fine.

The colleague's joke read the stool as a choice about engagement, when it was a choice about pain.

And Ollie read his own enthusiasm for the format as evidence that it worked for everyone, without asking the people for whom it might not.
moreCases.betterRead:
Bluedorn and colleagues found standing meetings shorter with no worse decisions, and Knight and Baer found groups without chairs shared information more readily, but these were short laboratory studies, and standing is not possible or comfortable for everyone. A format that forces one person to sit lower and further back than everyone else turns her into the overlooked seat of the room. Kirsty, after some thought, told Ollie about her condition. His better response, which he chose, was to change the format rather than ask her to fit it: he put a few high stools around the table for anyone who wanted one, used one himself on some mornings, and kept the fifteen-minute limit. Two other colleagues began using the stools too. Kirsty went back to speaking at the stand-ups, now at the same height as everyone else.

Ollie said later that he had learned more from the stool than from the research on standing meetings.

workedReading.title: Setting up a room for a contentious meeting
workedReading.scene:
Faisal, forty-six, is a council officer, and on Thursday evening he has to run a public meeting about a proposed cycle lane on a busy shopping street. Feelings are strong on both sides: shopkeepers worried about losing parking and trade, parents worried about their children cycling to school, older residents worried about crossing the road. About forty people have said they will come, and another dozen will join online. The community hall where the meeting is being held has been set up, as it always is, with a long top table at the front for the council officers and the local councillor, facing six rows of chairs. Faisal arrives an hour early and stands at the back of the hall, looking at the room as the residents will see it when they walk in.

He has run meetings like this before, in the same hall, set out the same way. They usually end with the officers defending a plan and the residents leaving angrier than they arrived. He wants to try something different, and the furniture is the one thing he can change in the next hour.

He also remembers a residents' meeting two years ago at which an older woman at the back gave up trying to speak and walked out.

steps.label: Read the room as set
steps.text:
From the back, the hall says one thing clearly: the council will speak and the residents will listen. The top table faces the rows like a stage. People in the back rows will see the backs of heads; people at the ends of each row will see the officers at an angle. The online participants will see whatever the single camera on the top table shows, which is the officers' faces and nothing of the room. If he leaves it like this, the meeting will turn into a queue of complaints aimed at the front.

He also notices the microphones. There is one fixed microphone on the top table and a single handheld one for the audience, which means the officers will be heard clearly and the residents will have to wait for a microphone to reach them.

steps.label: Take down the top table
steps.text:
With the caretaker's help, he moves the top table to the side, for the projector and the refreshments, and takes away the front-facing rows. He wants the officers to be part of the meeting, not facing it. Strodtbeck and Hook's research suggests that the people at the head of a room tend to be treated as its leaders and take more of the floor. Tonight he wants the residents to have more of it.

He also asks the caretaker for a second handheld microphone, so that residents on both sides of the room can speak without waiting for one to be passed across.

steps.label: Choose a shape
steps.text:
He arranges the chairs in two concentric horseshoes, open at one end, with a screen for the online participants at the open end, where everyone can see it. In a horseshoe, there is no head, almost everyone can see almost everyone else, and people tend to talk across the space to one another rather than only to the front. He leaves several chairs with arms at the ends of the rows for people who need them.

He leaves a wide gap in the outer horseshoe near the door, so that latecomers can join without walking across the middle, and puts a few chairs there with a clear view of the screen.

steps.label: Sit among them
steps.text:
He decides that he and the councillor will sit in the inner horseshoe, in different places, rather than together. That way the residents will not face a bloc of officials, and each official will be sitting beside residents. He puts the planning engineer, who will answer technical questions, in the middle of the inner row, with the widest view of the room, because she will need to catch eyes and answer quickly.

He also asks the councillor not to sit beside him, explaining that two officials side by side will look like a panel. She agrees, and chooses a seat between two of the shopkeepers.

steps.label: Watch who talks to whom
steps.text:
Once the meeting starts, he notices the Steinzor effect at work: people respond most to whoever is sitting opposite them across the horseshoe. A shopkeeper and a parent, facing each other, begin to argue. Faisal lets it run for a minute, then asks each of them to say what they would need to feel the plan was fair, and writes both answers on the flip chart, where everyone can see them side by side.

He also notices that the people sitting beside each other in the inner row, a parent and an older resident, start quietly comparing notes about the crossing. Side by side, they are on the same side of the problem.

steps.label: Bring in the edges
steps.text:
He keeps a list of the people who have not spoken. He looks to the outer horseshoe and the ends of the rows, where the quieter residents have sat, and invites them by name or by description: "I'd like to hear from someone who hasn't spoken yet, perhaps at this end." Every twenty minutes he turns to the screen and asks the online participants first, giving them a clear pause to unmute.

He also watches the screen for raised hands and the chat, and reads out one written question from an online participant who cannot speak because she is caring for a baby.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The meeting does not reach agreement, and Faisal did not expect it to. But it ends with a list of conditions that both the shopkeepers and the parents can live with, including a loading bay and a safer crossing near the school. Several residents tell him that it was the first council meeting they had been to where they felt listened to rather than talked at. One older man says he could actually see who was speaking. Faisal writes in his notes: no top table, horseshoe, officials scattered, screen at the open end, and a list of the silent.

He also notices that the online participants spoke more than at any previous meeting he has run, perhaps because the screen sat where the whole room could see it, and because he kept turning to it.

moreFailures.title: Using the seating plan as a weapon
moreFailures.body:
Once you know how much seating shapes a meeting, it is tempting to use that knowledge quietly against people: to put a critic in the seat beside the chair, where he can be overlooked, to seat an ally opposite you so that the exchanges flow your way, or to leave the newcomer on the chairs by the wall so that she will stay quiet. This is the meeting-room version of manipulation, and the ethics essay at the start of this book is clear about it: knowledge of how people read and respond to space should be used to include, not to steer people against their interests. It also tends to be noticed. People are often quicker to spot a rigged room than the person who rigged it expects. If you arrange seats, do it openly and for everyone's benefit, so that all can see and be seen, and be ready to say why.

Arranging a room so that one person's voice is quieter is still a way of silencing them, even if nobody can say that it happened.

moreFailures.title: Making a format compulsory
moreFailures.body:
New meeting formats are often introduced with enthusiasm and no exceptions: everyone stands, everyone sits on the floor for the workshop, everyone walks for the walking meeting. For many people, that is fine. For people with chronic pain, fatigue, a disability, a pregnancy, an injury, or simply a bad night, a compulsory format can mean either discomfort or being the visible exception, perched on a stool at the edge, as Kirsty was. Being the exception can become the overlooked seat. The fix is to build choice into the format from the start, so that nobody has to ask for it: chairs or stools around the standing table, a seated option for the walking meeting, a choice of seating at the workshop. Then let people use it without comment, and use it yourself sometimes, so that it is clearly normal.

It is also worth remembering that people may not tell you why a format is hard for them, as Kirsty did not at first. Choice built in means they do not have to.

A good test of any format is whether the person with the most difficulty can take part as fully as the person with the least.

moreFailures.title: Taking the same seat for ever
moreFailures.body:
Most people sit in the same place week after week, often from the first meeting they attended. Habit then fixes roles. The person who always sits at the end becomes the person who always sums up; the person who always sits beside the chair becomes the person nobody quite hears; the person who always sits by the door becomes the person who leaves early. Over time, everyone reads the pattern as character rather than geography. If you have been quiet in a meeting for months, try a different seat with a wider view and see whether it changes how often you speak and how you are answered. If you chair a regular meeting, occasionally mix the seating, openly and lightly, and watch whether different people come forward.

A new seat feels strange for a week or two. Give it three meetings before you decide whether it made a difference.

moreFailures.title: Leaving the laptop open
moreFailures.body:
An open laptop in a meeting draws the eyes of the person using it and, often, of the people around them. Sana, Weston and Cepeda found that students who multitasked on laptops in a lecture remembered less, and so did students sitting where they could see someone else's screen. In a meeting, the effect is social as well as cognitive: a person looking at a screen is a person not looking at the speaker, and the speaker can see it. A row of open laptops turns a meeting into a room of people half-elsewhere. Close the laptop unless you are presenting or genuinely need it for the item being discussed, and if you are taking notes on it, say so. If you chair, agree a simple norm at the start, rather than glaring at individuals halfway through.

The same goes for phones held under the table, which everyone can see and nobody mentions.

And if you need to check something urgently, step out briefly rather than half-attending at the table.

questions.q: Where should I sit if I want to be heard?
questions.a:
Where you can see, and be seen by, most of the people in the room. Howells and Becker found that leaders tended to emerge from the side of the table with the widest view of the group, and Strodtbeck and Hook found that people at the ends of a long table took part more. Avoid the seat immediately beside the chair, the far corners of a long side and the chairs against the wall, which are the easiest to overlook. Arriving a few minutes early gives you the choice. But use the knowledge to take part, not to compete for the best chair. If you notice that a quieter colleague always ends up on the edges, the best use of a good seat may be to offer it to them.

If you are new, arriving early is the easiest way to avoid the overlooked seats, because they are the ones left for latecomers.

questions.q: Where should I sit in a one-to-one meeting with my manager?
questions.a:
Often you will not have a choice, and that is fine. If you do, Sommer's work, discussed in Part I, suggests that sitting across a corner of a table, rather than directly opposite, tends to suit conversation, and that side by side suits working together on a document or a screen. Directly opposite, with a desk between you, tends to feel more formal and more like a negotiation or an assessment. If your manager always sits behind a desk and you sit in front of it, you could suggest moving to a small table for a particular conversation, such as a career discussion. Many managers are glad of the suggestion. The seat is not everything, but it can make a hard conversation easier to start.

If your manager always sits opposite you, it is worth noticing whether your conversations feel like assessments. A move to a corner can change that.

And if you are the manager, offering a choice of seat at the start of a hard conversation is a small courtesy that people notice.

questions.q: Is a round table really better?
questions.a:
In some ways. A round table has no head, so nobody gains the advantage of the end seat, and most people can see most others. That makes it easier for leadership to emerge from what people say rather than where they sit. But it does not remove geography altogether. Steinzor's finding that people respond most to whoever sits opposite still applies, and the person beside a dominant speaker can still be overlooked. Very large round tables can also make people across the table hard to hear. For small groups that need to discuss and decide together, a round or square table is often a good choice; for presentations, it may not be. What matters most is that everyone can see and be seen.

If you have a choice of room, a smaller table that comfortably fits everyone usually works better than a large one with empty chairs.

For some purposes. Bluedorn and colleagues found that standing meetings were about a third shorter than sitting ones, with no loss in decision quality, though people were less satisfied with them. Knight and Baer found that groups working in a room without chairs shared information more readily and were less territorial about their ideas. Both were short laboratory studies, so the results may not apply to long, complex discussions. Standing meetings tend to suit short, regular check-ins with a single purpose. They are not possible or comfortable for everyone, so offer chairs or stools as a normal part of the format, not as an exception, and ask people after a few weeks whether the meeting is better or simply shorter.

It also helps to give a standing meeting a firm end time and a single question, such as "What do you need from the rest of us today?"

questions.q: Should I ban phones and laptops from meetings?
questions.a:
A ban is often less useful than a shared norm. The evidence that a phone merely lying on the table spoils a conversation is weaker than popular articles suggest: Przybylski and Weinstein reported such an effect, but later attempts to repeat it did not find it. The evidence on open laptops is clearer, and suggests that screen use distracts the user and the people nearby. A sensible norm is that laptops stay closed unless someone is presenting or needs one for the item in hand, and phones stay face down or in bags unless someone is expecting an urgent call, in which case they say so. Agree it at the start of a regular meeting, follow it yourself, and revisit it if it is not working.

If you chair, close your own laptop first. People follow what the chair does far more than what the chair says.

questions.q: How can I run a fair hybrid meeting?
questions.a:
Treat the people on the screen as the most overlooked seats in the room and plan for them first. Some teams have everyone join from their own laptop, even those in the room, so that every face is the same size and every voice has its own microphone. If that is not possible, put the screen where the chair and most of the room can see it without turning, and use a good conference microphone. Ask remote participants for their views first on each item, or use a quick round of everyone, and leave a clear pause after asking. Some teams appoint a room buddy who watches the chat and the screen and speaks up for remote colleagues. And close each item by checking the screen before you move on.

It also helps to send papers in advance, so that remote participants are not trying to read a document over someone's shoulder on a shared screen.

After the meeting, ask one remote participant how it was for them. They will usually tell you exactly what to change.

watch.title: Dr. Strangelove: No Fighting in the War Room
watch.notice: A satirical war room built around a vast circular table. Notice how seating, light and distance from the centre shape who speaks and who is heard.

reviewPrompt: In your next meeting, map who sits where and who speaks, and bring in one person from an edge seat or the screen.
